Chapter 7: Overcoming the “Advice Monster”—Letting Go of the Need to Fix.
Have you ever caught yourself jumping in with advice before anyone even asks for it? That’s what we call the “advice monster.” It’s that reflex to offer solutions—sometimes just to show you’re helpful, or maybe to prove you know your stuff, or even to keep things under control.
But here’s the thing: when we give in to that urge, it can actually work against us. It can erode trust, shut down learning, and make people feel like they can’t think for themselves.
So, how do you let go of that advice monster? It all starts with self-awareness and a bit of honest practice. Try noticing what’s going on inside you when you feel that itch to jump in—maybe it’s a sense of urgency, a little frustration, or just being sure you’ve got the answer.
When you spot it, pause for a moment and ask yourself: “Is my input really needed right now? Or would asking a question be more helpful?”
Picture it this way: giving advice is like walking along a path you’ve traveled a hundred times. It’s easy, familiar, and you know exactly where it leads. But coaching? Coaching is more like stepping onto a brand-new trail. You don’t know what you’ll find, but the whole journey is full of discoveries—for you and for the person you’re with.
If you want to tame that advice monster, here are a few gentle reminders:
First, notice your triggers. Pay attention to the situations or emotions that make you want to leap in with advice.
Next, practice asking before telling. Try the Lazy Question—just ask, “How can I help?” and see what support is actually wanted.
Embrace silence, even if it feels awkward. Give people the space to think and respond in their own time.
And after your conversations, take a moment to reflect. Did sharing advice help? Or did asking questions lead to more engagement and fresh ideas?
Over time, you’ll notice something pretty amazing. When you let go of the urge to fix everything, you create more room for others to grow. People become more resourceful, more confident, and genuinely invested in figuring things out for themselves. And for you? There’s a lot less pressure to have all the answers, and a lot more satisfaction in seeing others succeed.
Imagine a project lead faced with a tough technical problem. Instead of prescribing the solution, they simply ask the team, “What options have you considered?” Right away, new ideas start to flow—and the team feels trusted and empowered.
Letting go of the advice monster is a process, and it takes patience and a little self-compassion. But each time you choose curiosity over giving advice, you’re building a culture where everyone learns and feels empowered.
